[[File:Circle_as_Lie_group.svg|thumb|Composition in the first unitary group]]
{{Short description|Special type of principal bundle}}
In [[mathematics]], especially [[differential geometry]], '''principal <math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math>-bundles''' (or '''principal <math>\operatorname{SO}(2)</math>-bundles''') are special [[Principal bundle|principal bundles]] with the first [[unitary group]] <math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math> ([[Isomorphism|isomorphic]] to the second [[special orthogonal group]] '''<math>\operatorname{SO}(2)</math>''') as [[structure group]]. Topologically, it has the structure of the one-dimensional [[sphere]], hence principal '''<math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math>'''-bundles without their group action are in particular [[Circle bundle|circle bundles]]. These are basically [[Topological space|topological spaces]] with a circle glued to every point, so that all of them are connected with each other, but globally aren't necessarily a [[Product topology|product]] and can instead be twisted like a [[Möbius strip]].

Principal <math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math>-bundles are used in many areas of mathematics, for example for the formulation of the [[Seiberg–Witten equations]] or [[monopole Floer homology]]. Since <math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math> is the [[Gauge group (mathematics)|gauge group]] of the [[electromagnetic interaction]], principal <math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math>-bundles are also of interest in [[theoretical physics]]. Concretely, the <math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math>-Yang–Mills equations are exactly [[Maxwell's equations]]. In particular, principal <math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math>-bundles over the two-dimensional [[sphere]] <math>S^2</math>, which include the complex [[Hopf fibration]], can be used to describe hypothetical [[Magnetic monopole|magnetic monopoles]] in three dimensions, known as [[Dirac monopole|Dirac monopoles]], see also [[two-dimensional Yang–Mills theory]].

== Definition ==
Principal <math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math>-bundles are generalizations of [[Canonical projection|canonical projections]] <math>B\times\operatorname{U}(1)\twoheadrightarrow B</math> for [[Topological space|topological spaces]] <math>B</math>, so that the source is not globally a product but only locally. More concretely, a continuous map <math>p\colon E\twoheadrightarrow B</math> with a continuous [[right group action]] <math>E\times\operatorname{U}(1)\rightarrow E</math>, which preserves all [[Preimage|preimages]] of points, hence  <math>p(eg)=p(e)</math> for all <math>e\in E</math> and <math>g\in G</math>, and also acts [[Free group action|free]] and [[Transitive group|transitive]] on all preimages of points, which makes all of them [[Homeomorphism|homeomorphic]] to <math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math>, is a principal <math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math>-bundle.<ref name=":7">Freed & Uhlenbeck 1984, p. 29</ref><ref name=":8">Mitchell 2001, p. 2</ref>

Since principal bundles are in particular fiber bundles with the group action missing, their nomenclature can be transferred. <math>E</math> is also called the ''total space'' and <math>B</math> is also called the ''base space''. Preimages of points are then the fibers. Since <math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math> is a [[Lie group]], hence in particular a [[smooth manifold]], the base space <math>B</math> is often chosen to be a smooth manifold as well since this automatically makes the total space <math>E</math> into a smooth manifold as well.

== Classification ==
Principal <math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math>-bundles can be fully classified using the [[Classifying space for U(n)|classifying space]] <math>\operatorname{BU}(1)</math> of the first unitary group <math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math>, which is exactly the infinite [[complex projective space]] <math>\mathbb{C}P^\infty\!</math>. For a [[topological space]] <math>B</math>, let <math>\operatorname{Prin}_{\operatorname{U}(1)}(B)</math> denote the set of [[Equivalence class|equivalence classes]] of principal <math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math>-bundles over it, then there is a [[bijection]] with [[homotopy classes]]:<ref name=":9">Mitchell 2011, Theorem 7.4</ref>

: <math>\operatorname{Prin}_{\operatorname{U}(1)}(B)
\cong[B,\operatorname{BU}(1)]
\cong[B,\mathbb{C}P^\infty].</math>

<math>\mathbb{C}P^\infty</math> is a [[CW complex]] with its <math>n</math>-skeleton being <math>\mathbb{C}P^k</math> for the largest [[natural number]] <math>k\in\mathbb{N}</math> with <math>2k\leq n</math>. For a <math>n</math>-dimensional CW complex <math>B</math>, the [[cellular approximation theorem]]<ref name=":3">Hatcher 2001, Theorem 4.8.</ref> states that every continuous map <math>B\rightarrow\mathbb{C}P^\infty</math> is homotopic to a cellular map factoring over the canonical inclusion <math>\mathbb{C}P^k\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}P^\infty\!</math>. As a result, the induced map <math>[B,\mathbb{C}P^k]\hookrightarrow[B,\mathbb{C}P^\infty]</math> is surjective, but not necessarily injective as higher cells of <math>\mathbb{C}P^\infty</math> allow additional homotopies. In particular if <math>B</math> is a CW complex of three or less dimensions, then <math>k=1</math> and with <math>\mathbb{C}P^1
\cong S^2</math>, there is a connection to [[Cohomotopy set|cohomotopy sets]] with a surjective map:

: <math>\pi^2(B)\rightarrow\operatorname{Prin}_{\operatorname{U}(1)}(B).</math>

<math>\mathbb{C}P^\infty</math> is also the [[Eilenberg–MacLane space]] <math>K(\mathbb{Z},2)</math>,<ref name=":1">Hatcher 2001, Example 4.50.</ref> which [[Representable functor|represents]] [[singular cohomology]],<ref name=":2">Hatcher 2001, Theorem 4.57.</ref> compare to [[Brown's representability theorem]]:

: <math>\operatorname{Prin}_{\operatorname{U}(1)}(B)
\cong H^2(B,\mathbb{Z}).</math>

(The composition <math>\pi^2(B)\rightarrow H^2(B,\mathbb{Z})</math> is the [[Hurewicz map]].) A corresponding isomorphism is given by the first [[Chern class]]. Although [[Characteristic class|characteristic classes]] are defined for [[Vector bundle|vector bundles]], it is possible to also define them for certain principal bundles.

== Associated vector bundle ==
Given a principal <math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math>-bundle <math>E\twoheadrightarrow B</math>, there is an associated [[vector bundle]] <math>
E\times_{\operatorname{U}(1)}\C\twoheadrightarrow B
</math>. Intuitively, the spheres at every point are filled over the canonical inclusions <math>\operatorname{U}(1)\subset\mathbb{C}</math>. Due to the single rank, the vector bundle is only described by the first [[Chern class]] <math>c_1\colon\operatorname{Vect}_\mathbb{C}(B)\rightarrow H^2(B,\mathbb{Z})</math>, which is an [[isomorphism]] over CW complexes.<ref name=":0">Hatcher 2017, Proposition 3.10.</ref>

Principal bundles also have an adjoint vector bundle, which is trivial for principal <math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math>-bundles.

== Examples ==

* By definition of [[complex projective space]], the canonical projection <math>S^{2n+1}\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb{C}P^n</math> is a principal <math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math>-bundle. With <math>\mathbb{C}P^1\cong S^2</math>, known as the [[Riemann sphere]], the complex [[Hopf fibration]] <math>h_\mathbb{C}\colon S^3\twoheadrightarrow S^2</math> is a special case. For the general case, the classifying map is the canonical inclusion:

:: <math>\mathbb{C}P^n\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}P^\infty
\cong\operatorname{BU}(1).</math>

* One has <math>S^{2n+1}
\cong\operatorname{U}(n+1)/\operatorname{U}(n)</math>, which means that there is a principal <math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math>-bundle  <math>\operatorname{U}(2)\twoheadrightarrow S^3\!</math>. Such bundles are classified by:<ref name=":10">Mitchell 2011, Corollary 11.2</ref>

:: <math>\pi_3\operatorname{BU}(1)
\cong\pi_2\operatorname{U}(1)
\cong\pi_2S^1
\cong 1.</math>
: Hence the bundle is trivial, which fits that <math>\operatorname{SU}(2)\cong S^3</math> and <math>\operatorname{U}(n)\cong\operatorname{SU}(n)\times\operatorname{U}(1)</math>.

* One has <math>S^n
\cong\operatorname{SO}(n+1)/\operatorname{SO}(n)</math>, which means that (using <math>\operatorname{U}(1)
\cong\operatorname{SO}(2)</math>) there is a principal <math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math>-bundle  <math>\operatorname{SO}(3)\twoheadrightarrow S^2</math>. Such bundles are classified by:<ref name=":10" />

:: <math>\pi_2\operatorname{BU}(1)
\cong\pi_1\operatorname{U}(1)
\cong\pi_1S^1
\cong\mathbb{Z}.</math>
: One has <math>\operatorname{SO}(3)\cong\mathbb{R}P^3</math> and the composition of the canonical double cover <math>S^3\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb{R}P^3</math> with the principal bundle <math>\mathbb{R}P^3\twoheadrightarrow S^2</math> is exactly the complex Hopf fibration <math>S^3\twoheadrightarrow S^2</math>. Since the first Chern class of the complex Hopf fibration is <math>-1</math>, the first Chern class of the principal bundle <math>\mathbb{R}P^3\twoheadrightarrow S^2</math> is <math>-2</math>.
